topic.title: What if the Mediterranean dried up? It already did once
topic.map_answer: one gap on the map, the Strait of Gibraltar: close it and the sea drains to a salt basin; open it and the Atlantic pours back in

title: Why would the Mediterranean turn into a salt desert?
description:
Why would the Mediterranean Sea turn into a desert of salt? It already did, once.
One gap at Gibraltar closed, the sun drained the sea to a salt basin, and then the Atlantic broke back in, all on the map.
Sources: Wikipedia (Nov 2026). The characters are not advisers.
Maps simplified. Borders as recognised by the country each video is about.
cta: Salt desert or blue sea: which Mediterranean would you visit? Comment

lines.text: Why would the Mediterranean Sea turn into a desert of salt?
It already did, once, and it all hangs on one gap at Gibraltar.
That gap is just 14.2 kilometres wide, the sea's only door to the open Atlantic Ocean.
The sun takes more water from this sea than its rivers bring, so the Atlantic keeps pouring in. So what if that door closed?
About 5.96M years ago, that door slammed shut.
Cut off, the sun took 3,300 cubic kilometres of water a year, and almost nothing came in to replace it.
Year after year, coast after coast, the water pulled back, leaving only salty lakes in the deepest basins.
Rivers like the Nile chased the falling water, carving deep canyons down to the new floor.
Until most of its 3.7M cubic kilometres were gone, leaving a salt desert kilometres deep. So how did the sea ever come back?
Then, about 5.33M years ago, the Atlantic broke back in at Gibraltar, spilling over the rock.
By one estimate it roared in at up to 100M cubic metres every second, filling the sea within two years.
Salt desert or blue sea: which would you visit? Because close that one gap again, and the sea starts to drain.

Re-review after 3 line changes (drain, shrink, break); the other 9 lines and all 6 facts are unchanged and were confirmed earlier on their Wikipedia pages (Messinian salinity crisis, Strait of Gibraltar, Zanclean flood). drain: 'almost nothing came in to replace it' fits the source's 3,300 km3/yr being NET evaporative loss after inflows. shrink: 'only salty lakes in the deepest basins' matches the source ('three or four large brine lakes on the abyssal plains remained'). break: 'spilling over the rock' matches the Zanclean page: water refilled the basin through the modern Strait of Gibraltar, the most widely accepted version being a stream eroding through the sill until it captured the Atlantic. Note: rivers still flowed in during the drying (canyon beat), so drain's 'almost nothing' is acceptable only because 3,300 is the net figure; style only.

No overlaps, cut-offs or placeholders; layout_problems empty; 61 s in the 60-80 range; audio -1.0/-16.2 dB as in the channel's shipped Shorts; disclaimer in the description; pick-one close and loop OK. All 6 facts confirmed on their Wikipedia pages via WebFetch: Messinian salinity crisis (start 5.96 +/- 0.02 Ma, 'precursor of the Strait of Gibraltar closed about 5.96 Ma'; ended with Gibraltar reopening 5.33 Ma; net evaporative loss ~3,300 km3/yr; 3.7 million km3 in the basin; no consensus on full drying, brine lakes remained -> script's 'most ... gone' and 'salty lakes' fit; Nile canyon cut ~2,500 m below sea level), Strait of Gibraltar infobox min width 14.2 km (body text says 14.3 km); evaporation exceeding river inflow confirmed; Zanclean flood: Garcia-Castellanos max ~100 million m3/s, 90% filled in months to two years, a modelled estimate attributed 'By one estimate'. Topic verify items met. Description ends with the channel disclaimer. Notes: at 5.96 Ma the connection was the strait's precursor / Betic-Rifian corridors (fine as a simplified map); 'slammed shut' is dramatic for a tectonic, repeated closure - style only.
